Race conditions exist in your reasoning

Joseph Halpern won the Gödel Prize for research on reasoning about knowledge and uncertainty. His insight is simply the way you think about what you know and what you don't know has the same logical structure as race conditions in concurrent systems. You can have conflicting beliefs about the state of reality at the same time. 

Understanding this changes how you debug distributed systems, how you think about consensus, how you reason about anything uncertain.

items.content:
RT @MsftSecIntel: Microsoft tracks Storm-3350, a Brazil-focused activity cluster observed since October, primarily affecting organizations in financial services, payments, banking, and digital assets. Microsoft-observed activity has also affected healthcare, transportation, and logistics.

Storm-3350 uses an identity-first cloud intrusion pattern that can begin with voice phishing (vishing) or identity-focused impersonation. In confirmed activity, the actor reset an account password through Microsoft’s legitimate self-service password-reset flow, signed in within minutes, completed the account’s existing SMS or voice multifactor authentication (MFA) challenge, and registered an actor-controlled Microsoft Authenticator method. This suggests an ability to intercept or receive codes sent to the registered phone number, potentially through social engineering involving employees’ personal phones. The new method provides persistent access without continued dependence on the victim or their phone.

After account takeover, Storm-3350 conducts reconnaissance and high-volume cloud-data collection across Microsoft Graph, Microsoft 365, and Azure, identifying high-value identities, applications, sites, drives, mailboxes, and sensitive content. This activity combines browser access with Python- and Node-style automation, OAuth-authenticated curl activity, and Azure CLI enumeration.

Storm-3350’s observed activity also included searching SharePoint for “AKIA” and accessing .key, .pem, and .ppk files. In Azure, the actor requested storage-account keys and application publishing profiles, which could enable access to additional cloud resources. Together, these actions point to possible routes beyond the compromised account. Defenders should investigate the full sequence rather than isolated events: password reset; immediate sign-in using existing MFA; authentication-method registration; anomalous token acquisition; Microsoft Graph and Azure control-plane reconnaissance; SharePoint, OneDrive, and mailbox discovery; sensitive-content searches; credential requests; and high-volume retrieval or download.

Relevant detections include:
- Suspicious Azure List Keys activities related to the List Keys operation
- Anomalous token acquisition followed by high-volume SharePoint file activity
- Graph API activity from a Microsoft threat intelligence IP address
- Mass SharePoint or OneDrive file access after an MFA method change
- Automated mass SharePoint/OneDrive file access via python-httpx
- Suspicious mass download from risky or unusual session

Microsoft tracks Storm-3350 separately within a broader financially motivated identity-compromise and cloud-data-theft ecosystem. Because related clusters share tactics, infrastructure patterns, and operational dependencies, no single IP, domain, or lure theme should be treated as conclusive actor attribution.

RT @igortsyg: A paper just published by  @DimitrisPapail @MSFTResearch shows how to backdoor any model and make it adversarial. All one needs is access to a tiny fraction of model’s weights. All open-weight models make their weights available. For proprietary models, access to weights may be gained via cyber activity.

Leading AI labs are starting to train their next-generation models. By their own estimates, they will achieve full Recursive Self-Improvement sometime in Q2 of next year. Even today, a larger and larger percentage of the models trained are done by machines, not humans.

It is well understood by the AI safety community that there are known risks in achieving “alignment.” What this means is that a model may perform malicious tasks such as hacking into other systems or manipulating environments or people to achieve its goal.

One such malicious task these models can easily perform is to backdoor and modify open-weight models or gain illicit access to proprietary weights of other models, as shown by the paper.

This may turn an arbitrary number of models running in the world today into malicious agents that have no human intent.

Today, we are already observing a very large and constantly growing number of malicious AI-driven attacks touching major institutions around the world. As posted before, these attacks may not match the intent of an attacker.

A combination of self-recursive, non-aligned training with large saturation of open-weight models across the world creates a toxic mix of global proportions.

We, as a society, should consider not allowing recursive self-improvement to commence until alignment is reasonably guaranteed.
